cim_eredeti: 5 Best Artificial Intelligence (AI) ETFs to Buy in 2026
szoveg_eredeti:
For investors, AI exchange-traded funds (ETFs) offer a simple way to get exposure to AI growth without relying on a single stock.

Artificial intelligence is no longer a futuristic concept. It's already shaping how companies operate and how consumers live. From recommendation engines and logistics software to chatbots and automation tools, AI is becoming a major driver of growth across tech, healthcare, finance, and other industries.

Rather than trying to pick individual winners, these funds group together companies that build AI technology or benefit from its adoption. That can include chipmakers, cloud platforms, software firms, and data-focused businesses.

Interest in AI investing remains strong as generative AI tools like ChatGPT push adoption into the mainstream. For investors seeking diversified exposure to AI’s long-term potential without the risk and research involved in picking individual stocks, AI ETFs can be a smart place to start.

Though the AI boom didn't begin in earnest until the launch of ChatGPT in late 2022, AI ETFs have been around for longer than that, with many investing in robotics, semiconductors, and related companies.

Among the top AI ETFs we'll look at in this article are the Global X Artificial Intelligence and Technology ETF, Global X Robotics and Artificial Intelligence ETF, Robo Global Robotics and Automation Index ETF, iShares Future AI and Tech ETF, and First Trust Nasdaq Artificial Intelligence and Robotics ETF.

Global X Artificial Intelligence and Technology ETF (AIQ -0.63%) is the largest AI ETF and a good first choice for investors looking for an AI ETF. The ETF launched in 2018 and aims to invest in companies that can benefit from the development of AI technology, as well as companies that make hardware used in AI, such as chips.

According to Global X, the global AI market is expected to grow from $184 billion in 2024 to $826.7 billion in 2030, suggesting the stocks in the fund should have significant growth ahead. Established in 2016, the Global X Robotics and Artificial Intelligence ETF (BOTZ -0.97%) is similar to the Global X Artificial Intelligence and Technology ETF but with a focus on robotics. The fund invests in "companies that potentially stand to benefit from increased adoption and utilization of robotics and artificial intelligence."

This includes enterprises working in industrial robotics, automation, non-industrial robots, and autonomous vehicles. According to Global X, the global robotics market was valued at more than $80 billion in 2022 and could grow to $280 billion by 2032.

The ETF held 81 stocks in November 2026, and its top five holdings made up more than 40% of the fund:

As the chart below shows, the ETF's shares have underperformed the S&P 500 index since its 2016 launch. The share price fell sharply in 2022, in line with the broad sell-off in tech stocks, but has since rebounded.

The ETF offered a modest trailing dividend yield of 0.54% in Nov. 2026, but it is better suited as a growth-oriented investment. It's an actively managed fund with an expense ratio of 0.68%, which is more than what you'd pay for most index funds.

The Robo Global Robotics and Automation Index ETF (ROBO -0.83%) focuses on companies driving "transformative innovations in robotics, automation, and artificial intelligence." This ETF invests in companies primarily focused on AI, cloud computing, and other technologies.

The ETF holds 79 stocks, with no single holding accounting for more than 2.5% of the ETF's value. Its top five holdings comprise only about 10% of the fund's total value. In Nov. 2026, its top five holdings include Intuitive Surgical, Fanuc, and three others:

Since its inception in 2013, the Robo ETF has underperformed the S&P 500, as the chart below shows. It trails the broad market index, with dividends factored into the return. The ETF pays a dividend yield of 0.39%, and its expense ratio is 0.95%. It primarily invests in companies focused on AI, cloud computing, and other technologies.

The iShares Future AI and Tech ETF (ARTY -0.73%) aims to track the results of an index of developed and emerging markets companies that could benefit from long-term opportunities in robotics and AI. The ETF was formed in 2018 and has about $3.7 billion in net assets.

With 50 stock holdings, it was well diversified in October 2026. Many of its top holdings also give investors exposure to fast-growing small-cap companies. The fund's top five investments as of October 2026 accounted for about 25% of the ETF's assets and included Nvidia, and four others:

As you can see from the chart below, the ETF has underperformed the S&P 500 for most of its history, but has recently outperformed it due to a surge in semiconductor stocks. The fund fell in 2022 when tech stocks crashed.

The expense ratio is competitive at 0.47%. The fund's performance will likely be heavily influenced by the overall performance of cloud and chip stocks, since they're the largest areas of exposure.

Though AI has been the dominant theme on the stock market for more than three years now, there hasn't been a related surge in AI ETFs.

The funds above have been active long before the launch of ChatGPT and offer exposure to both top AI chip stocks, like Nvidia, and lesser-known companies in areas like robotics, as well as international stocks.

ETF investors who are looking for exposure to AI stocks can also choose from adjacent funds like semiconductor ETFs, but for AI-specific ETFs, these five are the largest and most established.

AI ETFs have had mixed results in the stock market, as many of these funds fell sharply during the 2022 bear market.

By now, investors are familiar with the biggest names in the AI sector, like Nvidia, but if you're looking to get exposure to lesser-known, especially international ones, or in areas like robotics, AI ETFs can be a good choice.

AI ETFs can fit well into a diversified investment strategy, especially for investors new to the sector. AIQ, the biggest of the bunch, is a good place to start.
